advances: There are explicit rational mixed-integer convex bodies for which every point having relative depth at least \(e^{-n/64}\) in its own positive fiber has actual ambient halfspace depth \(o(2^{-n}W)\), uniformly over all fibers. This strengthens the obstruction to selecting actual fiber centroids: any point attaining a fixed positive multiple of \(2^{-n}W\) must eventually have exponentially small relative depth in its own fiber. The same bodies have explicitly specified rational points of actual depth at least \(\gamma_dW/4>W/(4e)\). A cube-pyramid variant also has a specified point of depth at least \(W/4\). These are obstructions to point-selection restrictions, not counterexamples to the locked conjecture. The parameterized construction includes the quadratic-roof simplex scales \(R=n^2\) and \(R=n^3\), their rational convex-hull versions, and positive dilations of the continuous coordinates.

proof:
The continuous centroid inequality used below is the one recorded and used in accepted fact \(\texttt{bb2b5f9519ae23e8}\): for a full-dimensional convex body \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), every closed halfspace containing \(\mathfrak c(K)\) has intersection volume at least \(\gamma_d\operatorname{vol}_d(K)\), where \(\gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d\). The elementary inequality \(\log(1+1/d)<1/d\) gives \(\gamma_d>e^{-1}\). All other estimates needed here are proved below.

First verify the exact bodies and fibers. If \(t\in[a,a+1]\), then the affine expression indexed by \(a\) is maximal in the definition of \(\phi_R\). Indeed, its difference from the expression indexed by \(b\), with the latter minus the former, is
\((b-a)(2t-a-b-1)\). This is nonpositive for both \(b>a\) and \(b<a\). Thus
\(\phi_R(t)=t^2+(t-a)(a+1-t)\) on that interval. In particular \(\phi_R\) is continuous and convex, \(\phi_R(t)\ge t^2\ge0\), and \(\phi_R(k)=k^2\) at every integer \(k\in[-R,R]\).

The sum \(\Phi_R\) is a maximum of finitely many affine functions with integer coefficients: choose one index \(a_i\) for each coordinate and sum the corresponding expressions. The roof inequalities defining the two bodies are therefore finite families of rational linear inequalities. The remaining inequalities are linear after resolving the absolute values. Both bodies are convex and closed. The simplex body lies in \([-R,R]^n\times[0,1]^d\). The cube body has \(0\le t\le d\) and \(|u_i|\le1/2\), so it is bounded as well. In the simplex body, \((\mathbf0,\mathbf1_d/(2d))\) satisfies every defining inequality strictly. In the cube body, \((\mathbf0,d/2,\mathbf0)\) does so. Hence both have nonempty interior in \(\mathbb R^{n+d}\).

At a lattice base within the box, \(\Phi_R(\mathbf z)=\|\mathbf z\|_2^2\). If this norm is larger than \(R\), neither body has a point over that base. If the norm is at most \(R\), the coordinate box is automatically satisfied, and direct substitution gives the stated fibers, including the singleton fibers at equality. Outside the box there are no fibers. This proves the entire support assertion without omitting zero-mass boundary bases.

Successive integration of the standard simplex gives \(\operatorname{vol}_d(A\Delta_d)=A^d/d!\). Its centroid is the average of its \(d+1\) vertices, hence \(A\mathbf1_d/(d+1)\). One can justify the latter formula directly by permuting its \(d+1\) barycentric coordinates: their integrals are equal and their sum is one. For the cube pyramid, integrating its cross-sectional \((d-1)\)-volume gives
\[
\int_{\Psi(\mathbf z)}^d(1-t/d)^{d-1}\,dt=A_{\mathbf z}^d.
\]
Reflection in each \(u_i\) gives zero centroid coordinates in \(\mathbf u\). Under the substitution \(t=\Psi(\mathbf z)+(d-\Psi(\mathbf z))v\), its normalized height density is \(d(1-v)^{d-1}\) on \([0,1]\). Its mean is \(1/(d+1)\), since \(\int_0^1v(1-v)^{d-1}\,dv=1/[d(d+1)]\). This proves the centroid formula. The simplex fibers are homothetic about \(\mathbf0\); the cube fibers are homothetic about \((d,\mathbf0)\), in both cases by factor \(A_{\mathbf z}\) from the fiber at zero. All factors lie in \([0,1]\), so the fibers are nested. The asserted function \(f\) agrees with the weights on every lattice base. On its positive ball, \(1-\|\mathbf x\|_2^2/R^2\) is positive and concave, so its logarithm is concave by composition with the increasing concave logarithm. Extending \(f\) by zero preserves the log-concavity inequality, because its positive support is convex and any zero factor makes the inequality's right side zero.

A boundary fiber cannot hide a positive-depth point. If \(\mathbf j\in D\setminus D_+\), then \(\|\mathbf j\|_2=R\). The closed halfspace with base inequality \(\mathbf j\cdot\mathbf x\ge R^2\) contains the whole fiber at \(\mathbf j\). Among nonempty lattice bases, Cauchy--Schwarz shows that equality or a larger value is possible only at \(\mathbf z=\mathbf j\). This halfspace therefore has mixed volume zero, since that fiber has zero \(d\)-volume.

We next prove a lower bound for \(W\) that is uniform over the two shapes. In the remainder of this paragraph assume \(n\ge20\). For either body, \(w_{\mathbf z}=v_0A_{\mathbf z}^d\) on \(D_+\), where \(v_0=1/d!\) for the simplex and \(v_0=1\) for the cube. For \(0\le v<1\), integration of \(t/(1-t)\) gives
\[
-\log(1-v)-v
=\int_0^v\frac{t}{1-t}\,dt
\le\frac{v^2}{2(1-v)}.
\]
Consequently, if \(0\le u\le n\) and \(d=n^2\), then
\[
d\log(1-u/d)
\ge-u-\frac{u^2}{2d(1-u/d)}
\ge-u-1,
\qquad
(1-u/d)^d\ge e^{-u-1}.
\]
The last error term is at most \(1/[2(1-1/n)]\le1\).

The Gaussian integral equals \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-s^2}\,ds=\sqrt\pi\): squaring the integral and using polar coordinates gives its square as \(2\pi\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2}\,dr=\pi\). Integration by parts also gives \(\int_{\mathbb R}s^2e^{-s^2}\,ds=\sqrt\pi/2\). It follows by products and scaling that the probability density proportional to \(e^{-\Psi(\mathbf x)}\) has normalizing integral \((\sqrt\pi L)^n\) and expectation of \(\Psi\) equal to \(n/2\). Therefore, on \(U=\{\mathbf x:\Psi(\mathbf x)\le3n/4\}\), Markov's inequality gives
\[
\int_U e^{-\Psi(\mathbf x)}\,d\mathbf x
\ge\frac13(\sqrt\pi L)^n.
\]
Round the coordinates of \(\mathbf x\in U\) to a nearest lattice vector \(\mathbf z\). Since the rounding distance is at most \(\sqrt n/2\),
\[
\Psi(\mathbf z)
\le \Psi(\mathbf x)+\frac{\sqrt{3}n}{2L}+\frac{n}{4L^2}
\le \Psi(\mathbf x)+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac1{4n}
< \Psi(\mathbf x)+1\le n.
\]
Here \(L\ge n\), \(n\ge20\), and \(\sqrt3<7/4\) justify the strict error bound. The rounded base is in \(D_+\), and the preceding logarithmic estimate gives
\(A_{\mathbf z}^d\ge e^{-\Psi(\mathbf z)-1}\ge e^{-\Psi(\mathbf x)-2}\).
Choose a fixed rule at rounding ties. The unit rounding cells have disjoint interiors and volume one. Integrating this inequality on their intersections with \(U\) proves
\[
\frac W{v_0}
\ge e^{-2}\int_U e^{-\Psi(\mathbf x)}\,d\mathbf x
\ge\frac{e^{-2}}3(\sqrt\pi L)^n.
\]

For later counting, write \(\kappa_n=\operatorname{vol}_n(B_2^n)\). The unit cubes about lattice points in any ball of radius \(r\) have disjoint interiors and lie in the concentric ball of radius \(r+\sqrt n/2\). Hence their number is at most \(\kappa_n(r+\sqrt n/2)^n\). Also,
\[
e^{-n/2}\kappa_n
\le\int_{B_2^n}e^{-n\|\mathbf x\|_2^2/2}\,d\mathbf x
\le\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)^{n/2},
\qquad
\kappa_n\le\left(\frac{2\pi e}{n}\right)^{n/2}.
\]
Thus neither lattice-count estimate requires an asymptotic approximation.

Consider now any \(\mathbf p=(\mathbf j,\mathbf y)\) in a positive simplex fiber, and set \(s=\sum_i y_i\). The own-fiber halfspace \(\sum_i v_i\le s\) contains \(\mathbf y\), and its fiber volume is exactly \(s^d/d!\), since \(0\le s\le A_{\mathbf j}\). If \(\alpha_C(\mathbf p)\ge\alpha>0\), it follows that
\[
\left(\frac{s}{A_{\mathbf j}}\right)^d\ge\alpha,
\qquad
A_{\mathbf j}-s\le1-\alpha^{1/d}
\le\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}d.
\]
The last inequality is \(1-e^{-a}\le a\) for \(a\ge0\). The closed ambient halfspace
\[
H_{\mathbf p}
=\left\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf v):
\sum_i v_i\ge s-\frac{2\mathbf j\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf j)}{R^2}\right\}
\]
has \(\mathbf p\) on its boundary. At any nonempty lattice fiber, its threshold and the fiber roof satisfy the exact identity
\[
A_{\mathbf z}
-\left(s-\frac{2\mathbf j\cdot(\mathbf z-\mathbf j)}{R^2}\right)
=A_{\mathbf j}-s-\frac{\|\mathbf z-\mathbf j\|_2^2}{R^2}.
\]
A negative right side means the intersection is empty. Equality confines the intersection to the hyperplane \(\sum_i v_i=A_{\mathbf z}\), which has zero \(d\)-volume, also when the fiber is a singleton. Thus positive volume requires
\(\|\mathbf z-\mathbf j\|_2<L\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\).

For a cube-fiber point \(\mathbf p=(\mathbf j,t,\mathbf u)\), the own-fiber cap with height at least \(t\) has volume \((1-t/d)^d\). Put \(s=1-t/d\). Then \(0\le s\le A_{\mathbf j}\), and the same relative-depth hypothesis gives \(A_{\mathbf j}-s\le\log(1/\alpha)/d\). Use instead the ambient halfspace
\[
H_{\mathbf p}
=\left\{(\mathbf x,t',\mathbf v):
t'\le t+\frac{2\mathbf j\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf j)}{L^2}\right\}.
\]
At base \(\mathbf z\), its upper height minus the fiber's lower height is
\[
t+\frac{2\mathbf j\cdot(\mathbf z-\mathbf j)}{L^2}-\Psi(\mathbf z)
=t-\Psi(\mathbf j)-\frac{\|\mathbf z-\mathbf j\|_2^2}{L^2}
=d(A_{\mathbf j}-s)-\frac{\|\mathbf z-\mathbf j\|_2^2}{L^2}.
\]
Equality confines the section to a single height and gives zero \(d\)-volume; a negative value gives the empty section. Positive volume again requires the same strict radius bound. These are actual ambient halfspaces through the chosen points, for every positive fiber and every continuous point satisfying the local-depth condition.

Every contributing fiber in either family has mass at most \(v_0\). The lattice count and the lower bound for \(W\) therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2^n h_S(\mathbf p)}W
&\le
3e^2\frac{2^n\kappa_n
\bigl(L\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}+\sqrt n/2\bigr)^n}
{(\sqrt\pi L)^n}\\
&\le3e^2\left[
2\sqrt{2e}\left(
\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}n}+\frac1{2L}\right)\right]^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the pointwise bound. Since \(e<3\) and therefore \(2\sqrt{2e}<5\), substituting \(\alpha=e^{-n/64}\), \(L\ge n\), and \(n\ge20\) bounds the bracket by
\(5(1/8+1/40)=3/4\).

We next prove the weighted-median conclusions, initially for every \(n\ge2\). All weights and all positive \(A_{\mathbf z}\) are rational, and the support is finite and nonempty. The specified smallest attained median exists and is rational. Its lower-side weight is at least \(W/2\); minimality says the weight strictly below it is less than \(W/2\), which proves the asserted upper-side inequality, including ties. Both sides are centrally symmetric in the base and paired bases have equal weights.

Let \(\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}}\) denote the common continuous apex, namely \(\mathbf0\) for the simplex and \((d,\mathbf0)\) for the cube. If \(\mathbf c_{\mathbf0}\) is the centroid of the fiber at zero, both fiber tables have
\(\mathbf c_{\mathbf z}=\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}}+A_{\mathbf z}(\mathbf c_{\mathbf0}-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}})\).
The specified point has continuous coordinate
\(\mathbf y_* =\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}}+\rho(\mathbf c_{\mathbf0}-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}})\),
so it is the centroid of the homothetic body
\(K_\rho=\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}}+\rho(C_{\mathbf0}-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}})\subseteq C_{\mathbf0}\).
This also proves \(\mathbf p_*\in S\).

Take any proper closed halfspace through \(\mathbf p_*\), written as
\(H=\{(\mathbf z,\mathbf y):\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf z+\boldsymbol\beta\cdot(\mathbf y-\mathbf y_*)\ge0\}\).
Its defining expression at a fiber centroid is
\(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf z+b(A_{\mathbf z}-\rho)\), where
\(b=\boldsymbol\beta\cdot(\mathbf c_{\mathbf0}-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ap}})\).
The set of bases with \(b(A_{\mathbf z}-\rho)\ge0\) has weight at least \(W/2\); when \(b=0\) it is all of \(D_+\). It is centrally symmetric. At least half its weight has \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf z\ge0\), including any fixed point of the reflection. Every corresponding fiber centroid lies in \(H\). If \(\boldsymbol\beta\ne\mathbf0\), its fiber section is a proper closed halfspace containing that centroid, so the accepted centroid inequality contributes at least \(\gamma_dw_{\mathbf z}\). If \(\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf0\), the section at every selected base is the whole continuous space and the same lower bound holds. Summing gives \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\ge\gamma_dW/4\).

Any proper closed halfspace containing a point contains its parallel sub-halfspace whose boundary passes through that point: if its defining inequality is \(\ell\ge a\), replace \(a\) by the value of \(\ell\) at the point. The whole-space case, if included in the halfspace convention, is immediate. Therefore the preceding lower bound holds for all containing halfspaces and proves the actual depth claim.

The centroid inequality applied to \(K_\rho\) gives relative own-fiber depth at least \(\gamma_d\rho^d\) at \(\mathbf p_*\). For the simplex fiber at zero, the containing cap \(\sum_i y_i\le d\rho/(d+1)\) has precisely the fraction \((d\rho/(d+1))^d=\gamma_d\rho^d\). For the cube fiber at zero, the containing cap \(t\ge d-d^2\rho/(d+1)\) has exactly that same fraction, by the cross-sectional integral already computed. These matching upper bounds prove \(\alpha_C(\mathbf p_*)=\gamma_d\rho^d\). The identical argument with \(\rho=1\), followed by the homothety from the fiber at zero to any positive fiber, proves that every fiber centroid has relative depth exactly \(\gamma_d\).

For \(n\ge20\), the small-base ball carries less than half the mass. Indeed, the unit-cube count and the established Gaussian lower bound give
\[
\frac{\sum_{\Psi(\mathbf z)\le n/16}w_{\mathbf z}}W
\le3e^2\left[
\sqrt{2e}\left(\frac14+\frac1{2L}\right)\right]^n
<27\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^n<\frac12.
\]
For the first strict numerical bound use \(e<3\), \(\sqrt{2e}<5/2\), and \(L\ge n\ge20\). For the second, \((11/16)^4=14641/65536<1/4\), so \(27(11/16)^n\le27(11/16)^{20}<27/1024<1/2\). If \(\rho\ge1-1/(16n)\), the median's upper side would be contained in \(\{\Psi\le n/16\}\), contradicting its weight being at least \(W/2\). Thus \(\rho<1-1/(16n)\), and
\(\gamma_d\rho^d<\gamma_d(1-1/(16n))^{n^2}\le\gamma_de^{-n/16}\).
In particular \(\rho<1\), so \(\mathbf p_*\) differs from the centroid of its fiber at zero and, by its base coordinate, from every other fiber centroid.

The pointwise bound now gives the asserted centroid asymptotics: \(\log(1/\gamma_d)=d\log(1+1/d)<1\), so its bracket is at most \(2\sqrt{2e}(n^{-1/2}+1/(2L))\), which tends to zero uniformly in \(L\ge n\). For \(n\ge1024\), this bracket is less than
\(5(1/32+1/2048)=325/2048<1/4\).
Thus \(2^nh_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))/W<3e^2\,4^{-n}<3\,2^{-n}\), where \(e^2<9<2^n\) gives the last inequality. Dividing by \(2^n\) proves \(h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))<3\,4^{-n}W\).

For the stronger cube point, the mixed volume at heights at most \(t\in[0,d]\) is
\[
F(t)=\sum_{\mathbf z\in D_+}
\left(A_{\mathbf z}^d-(1-t/d)^d\right)_+.
\]
This follows by integrating the cube cross-sections from \(\Psi(\mathbf z)\) to \(t\) when \(\Psi(\mathbf z)<t\), and assigning zero otherwise. It is continuous, \(F(0)=0\), and \(F(d)=W\). The contribution of the zero base, \(1-(1-t/d)^d\), is strictly increasing on \([0,d]\), so \(F\) is strictly increasing. The specified \(\tau\) therefore exists uniquely and lies in \((0,d)\). The point \((\mathbf0,\tau,\mathbf0)\) belongs to the fiber at zero.

For each \(t\in(0,d)\), the mixed section in the remaining coordinates is the product of the lattice set \(\{\mathbf z:\Psi(\mathbf z)\le t\}\) and the cube \([-(1-t/d)/2,(1-t/d)/2]^{d-1}\), equipped with counting measure times Lebesgue measure. It is invariant under \((\mathbf z,\mathbf u)\mapsto(-\mathbf z,-\mathbf u)\). Consider a proper closed halfspace through \(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{height}}\), written as
\(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf z+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf u+c(t-\tau)\ge0\).
Whenever \(c(t-\tau)\ge0\), the contained set includes \(\{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf z+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf u\ge0\}\), which has at least half of that section's measure by reflection, also when there is boundary mass. If \(c>0\), integrate over \(t\ge\tau\); if \(c<0\), integrate over \(t\le\tau\). Each range has total mixed volume \(W/2\), since \(F\) is continuous. If \(c=0\), the half-section estimate holds at every height. In every case, Fubini's theorem gives a halfspace mass at least \(W/4\). The parallel-sub-halfspace argument extends this to every containing halfspace.

When \(n\ge20\), this point is not the centroid at zero. That centroid has height \(d/(d+1)<1\le n/16\). Its lower-height mass is at most \(\sum_{\Psi(\mathbf z)\le n/16}w_{\mathbf z}<W/2\), by the small-ball estimate above. Consequently \(\tau>d/(d+1)\). Its base zero again excludes equality with a centroid on any other fiber.

It remains to verify the original even-\(n\) constants and its closed-form point for the full stated range \(n\ge2\), without using the \(n\ge20\) estimates. Take the simplex body with \(L=n^2\) and \(R=n^3\). At a fiber centroid the previously constructed simplex halfspace has \(s=dA_{\mathbf j}/(d+1)\), so a positive contribution requires
\[
\|\mathbf z-\mathbf j\|_2^2
<\frac{R^2 A_{\mathbf j}}{d+1}
<L^2.
\]
Every fiber has mass at most \(1/d!\), whence
\(h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))\le\kappa_n(L+\sqrt n/2)^n/d!\).
Every integer \(\mathbf z\in[-L,L]^n\) has \(A_{\mathbf z}\ge1-1/n>0\). There are exactly \((2L+1)^n\) such bases, giving
\[
W\ge\frac{(2L+1)^n(1-1/n)^{n^2}}{d!},
\qquad
\frac{h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))}{2^{-n}W}
\le\kappa_n\left(\frac{2L+\sqrt n}{2L+1}\right)^n(1-1/n)^{-n^2}.
\]
Here
\(n\log((2L+\sqrt n)/(2L+1))\le n\sqrt n/(2L)=1/(2\sqrt n)\).
Also \(-\log(1-u)\le u/(1-u)\) for \(0\le u<1\), by integrating \(1/(1-t)\). Thus
\(-n^2\log(1-1/n)\le n^2/(n-1)\le n+2\).
Using the proved bound on \(\kappa_n\) and \(2+1/(2\sqrt n)\le3\) gives
\[
\frac{h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))}{2^{-n}W}
\le e^3\left(\frac{2\pi e^3}{n}\right)^{n/2}.
\]
This is uniform in all \(\mathbf j\in D_+\); its logarithm is at most \(3+(n/2)(\log(2\pi e^3)-\log n)\), which tends to minus infinity.

Put \(q_n=1-1/(2n)\) and \(E=\{\mathbf z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|\mathbf z\|_2\le L\sqrt{n/2}\}\). Every base in \(E\) is positive and has \(A_{\mathbf z}\ge q_n\), so its fiber contains \(q_n\Delta_d\). These inner simplexes share centroid \(q_n\mathbf1_d/(d+1)\). The set \(E\) is centrally symmetric. For any halfspace through \(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{exp}}\), at least half the bases in \(E\) have their common-inner-simplex centroid in the corresponding section, by pairing bases \(\mathbf z,-\mathbf z\). The accepted centroid inequality, with the whole-section case included as before, consequently gives
\[
h_S(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{exp}})
\ge\frac{\gamma_d|E|q_n^d}{2d!}.
\]

We prove the needed comparison with \(W\). Since \((1-u)^d\le e^{-du}\),
\[
Wd!\le\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\|\mathbf z\|_2^2/L^2}
=\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty e^{-k^2/L^2}\right)^n
\le(1+L\sqrt\pi)^n.
\]
The last step uses that the summand decreases with \(k\): its sum over positive integers is at most \(\int_0^\infty e^{-t^2/L^2}\,dt=L\sqrt\pi/2\). Conversely, the unit cubes centered at points of \(E\) cover the ball of radius \(L\sqrt{n/2}-\sqrt n/2\), because rounding a point in this smaller ball reaches a base in \(E\). Hence
\(|E|\ge\kappa_n(L\sqrt{n/2}-\sqrt n/2)^n\).

Write \(n=2m\). The exact ball-volume formula \(\kappa_{2m}=\pi^m/m!\) follows by integrating the last two coordinates in polar form: \(\kappa_{2m}=2\pi\kappa_{2m-2}\int_0^1r(1-r^2)^{m-1}\,dr=(\pi/m)\kappa_{2m-2}\), starting at \(\kappa_0=1\). Therefore
\[
\frac{|E|}{Wd!}
\ge\frac{m^m}{m!}
\left(\frac{1-1/(\sqrt2L)}{1+1/(\sqrt\pi L)}\right)^n
\ge\frac{m^m}{m!}e^{-3/2}.
\]
To check the final constant, put \(u=1/(\sqrt2L)\) and \(v=1/(\sqrt\pi L)\). Both are at most \(1/L\le1/4\), and
\[
n\bigl[-\log(1-u)+\log(1+v)\bigr]
\le n\left(\frac{u}{1-u}+v\right)
\le\frac{7n}{3L}
=\frac7{3n}\le\frac32.
\]
Also
\(-d\log q_n\le n^2/(2n-1)\le n/2+1/2=m+1/2\), so \(q_n^d\ge e^{-m-1/2}\). Since \(\log t\) is increasing,
\[
\log(m!)\le\int_1^m\log t\,dt+\log m
=m\log m-m+1+\log m,
\qquad
\frac{m^m}{m!}\ge\frac{e^{m-1}}m.
\]
These formulas include \(m=1\). Combining them with \(\gamma_d>1/e\) proves
\[
\frac{h_S(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{exp}})}W
\ge\frac1{2e}\frac{e^{m-1}}{m}e^{-3/2}e^{-m-1/2}
=\frac1{e^4n}.
\]
The point is in the fiber at zero and differs from its centroid because \(q_n<1\). Finally \(2^n\ge2n\) for every integer \(n\ge2\), starting with equality at \(n=2\) and following by induction, which gives the displayed weak-Oertel-scale lower bound.

The convex-hull realization needs no interpolation assumption beyond what was proved. Every listed generating vertex of \(\widehat C^\Delta_{n,L}\) lies in \(C^\Delta_{n,L}\). Convexity gives \(\widehat C^\Delta_{n,L}\subseteq C^\Delta_{n,L}\). Conversely, for each \(\mathbf z\in D\) its generating vertices contain the whole prescribed simplex \(\{\mathbf z\}\times A_{\mathbf z}\Delta_d\). These two inclusions prove equality of every integer fiber, including the zero and empty ones. The convex hull is a rational polytope because the finite generating vertices are rational. It is full-dimensional: it contains \((\mathbf0,\mathbf0)\), the \(n\) points \((\mathbf e_i,\mathbf0)\) in the base directions, and the \(d\) points \((\mathbf0,\mathbf e_j)\) in the continuous directions, an affinely independent set. Thus this realization has the identical mixed-integer set \(S\).

The substitution of the quadratic roof for the piecewise-affine roof changes no integer fiber, because \(\Phi_R(\mathbf z)=\|\mathbf z\|_2^2\) at every relevant lattice base. Under the continuous dilation by \(\lambda>0\), halfspaces correspond bijectively by inverse image. All \(d\)-dimensional fiber intersection volumes and \(W\) are multiplied by \(\lambda^d\). This proves the stated invariance of both depth normalizations and transports every witness; rational dilation preserves rational defining data.

For any fixed \(c_0>0\), choose \(n\) large enough that \(3e^2(3/4)^n<c_0\). The all-locally-deep-point bound then excludes every positive-fiber point with \(\alpha_C\ge e^{-n/64}\) from attaining \(c_0 2^{-n}W\). The zero-volume fibers have already been excluded by their zero ambient depths. At the same time the rational weighted-median points have actual depth at least \(\gamma_dW/4\). This proves the claimed obstruction with the precise quantifiers and confirms that it does not disprove the locked conjecture.
statement:
Let \(n\ge2\) and \(L\ge n\) be integers, and put \(d=n^2\) and \(R=nL\), so \(R^2=dL^2\). For \(-R\le t\le R\), define
\[
\phi_R(t)=\max_{a\in\{-R,\ldots,R-1\}}
\bigl((2a+1)t-a(a+1)\bigr),
\qquad
\Phi_R(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_R(x_i).
\]
Let \(\Delta_d=\{\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^d:\mathbf y\ge\mathbf0,\ \sum_{i=1}^d y_i\le1\}\). Consider the two bodies
\[
\begin{aligned}
C^\Delta_{n,L}
&=\left\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf y):
\mathbf x\in[-R,R]^n,\quad \mathbf y\ge\mathbf0,\quad
\sum_{i=1}^d y_i+\frac{\Phi_R(\mathbf x)}{R^2}\le1\right\},\\
C^\square_{n,L}
&=\left\{(\mathbf x,t,\mathbf u):
\mathbf x\in[-R,R]^n,\quad
\frac{\Phi_R(\mathbf x)}{L^2}\le t\le d,\quad
|u_i|\le\frac12\left(1-\frac td\right)\ (1\le i\le d-1)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the second body the continuous vector is \(\mathbf y=(t,\mathbf u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Both bodies are compact, full-dimensional rational polytopes.

For either choice \(C\), use the canonical quantities
\(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\),
\(C_{\mathbf z}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf z,\mathbf y)\in C\}\),
\(w_{\mathbf z}=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_{\mathbf z})\),
\(D_+=\{\mathbf z:w_{\mathbf z}>0\}\), and
\(W=\sum_{\mathbf z}w_{\mathbf z}=\mathcal H_d(S)\).
Write \(\mathbf c_{\mathbf z}=\mathfrak c(C_{\mathbf z})\) on \(D_+\), and use the locked problem's actual ambient halfspace depth \(h_S\). These agree with accepted fact \(\texttt{bb2b5f9519ae23e8}\); its continuous coordinate \(\mathbf x\) is called \(\mathbf y\) here, while \(\mathbf x\) denotes the base coordinate. Its continuous halfspace variable \(L\) is denoted \(J\) below; here \(L\) is the integer construction scale. The alternative fiber-mass notation \(a_{\mathbf z}\) means \(w_{\mathbf z}\); the alternative radius notation \(r_{\mathbf z}\) means \(A_{\mathbf z}\) below; and \(h_C\) and \(W_n\) mean \(h_S\) and \(W\) for the indicated body. The normalized quadratic function called \(Q\) in the smaller-scale formulation is denoted \(\Psi\) here. No centroid-graph certificate is being used as a substitute for \(h_S\).

Put \(\Psi(\mathbf x)=\|\mathbf x\|_2^2/L^2\) and \(A_{\mathbf z}=1-\Psi(\mathbf z)/d\). The complete nonempty lattice support is
\(D=\{\mathbf z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|\mathbf z\|_2\le R\}\), and
\(D_+=\{\mathbf z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|\mathbf z\|_2<R\}\).
For \(\mathbf z\in D_+\), the exact fiber data are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(C^\Delta_{n,L})_{\mathbf z}&=A_{\mathbf z}\Delta_d,
&w_{\mathbf z}&=\frac{A_{\mathbf z}^d}{d!},
&\mathbf c_{\mathbf z}&=\frac{A_{\mathbf z}}{d+1}\mathbf1_d,\\
(C^\square_{n,L})_{\mathbf z}
&=\left\{(t,\mathbf u):\Psi(\mathbf z)\le t\le d,\quad
|u_i|\le\frac12(1-t/d)\right\},
&w_{\mathbf z}&=A_{\mathbf z}^d,
&\mathbf c_{\mathbf z}&=\left(\Psi(\mathbf z)+\frac{d-\Psi(\mathbf z)}{d+1},\mathbf0\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\mathbf z\in D\setminus D_+\), the fibers are respectively \(\{\mathbf0\}\) and \(\{(d,\mathbf0)\}\); they have zero \(d\)-volume. All fibers outside \(D\) are empty. Every point in a zero-volume fiber has actual ambient depth zero. In each family the positive fibers are nested homothetic pyramids with a common apex, and their centroids lie on one continuous-coordinate line. Writing \(v_0=w_{\mathbf0}\), each weight table has the finite-valued, globally log-concave extension
\(f(\mathbf x)=v_0(1-\|\mathbf x\|_2^2/R^2)_+^d\), including every zero lattice value. Here \(a_+=\max(a,0)\).

For \(\mathbf p=(\mathbf j,\mathbf y)\in S\) with \(\mathbf j\in D_+\), define its relative depth in its own fiber by
\[
\alpha_C(\mathbf p)=\frac1{w_{\mathbf j}}
\inf\left\{\operatorname{vol}_d(C_{\mathbf j}\cap J):
J\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is a closed halfspace and }\mathbf y\in J\right\}.
\]
For \(n\ge20\), every \(0<\alpha\le1\) and every such point with \(\alpha_C(\mathbf p)\ge\alpha\) satisfy
\[
\frac{h_S(\mathbf p)}{2^{-n}W}
\le3e^2\left[
2\sqrt{2e}\left(
\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}n}+\frac1{2L}
\right)\right]^n.
\]
Consequently, uniformly in integer \(L\ge n\), every point with \(\alpha_C(\mathbf p)\ge e^{-n/64}\) satisfies
\[
\frac{h_S(\mathbf p)}{2^{-n}W}
\le3e^2\left(\frac34\right)^n\longrightarrow0.
\]
Every positive-fiber centroid has relative own-fiber depth exactly
\(\gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d\). In particular all actual centroid depths, divided by \(2^{-n}W\), tend uniformly to zero. For either family, the explicit bound
\(h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))<3\,4^{-n}W\)
holds for every \(\mathbf j\in D_+\) when \(n\ge1024\).

There is also a rational point with constant actual relative depth. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest attained value in \(\{A_{\mathbf z}:\mathbf z\in D_+\}\) for which \(\sum_{A_{\mathbf z}\le\rho}w_{\mathbf z}\ge W/2\). Thus
\[
\sum_{A_{\mathbf z}\le\rho}w_{\mathbf z}\ge\frac W2,
\qquad
\sum_{A_{\mathbf z}\ge\rho}w_{\mathbf z}\ge\frac W2.
\]
The weighted-median radius called \(t_n\) in the simplex formulation is \(\rho\) here; it is distinct from the cube's height coordinate \(t\). The two weight tables differ by a constant factor, so they give the same \(\rho\). Define
\[
\mathbf p^\Delta_*=
\left(\mathbf0,\frac{\rho}{d+1}\mathbf1_d\right),
\qquad
\mathbf p^\square_*=
\left(\mathbf0,d-\frac{d^2\rho}{d+1},\mathbf0\right).
\]
For all \(n\ge2\) and \(L\ge n\), the appropriate point belongs to its body's \(S\) and satisfies
\[
h_S(\mathbf p_*)\ge\frac{\gamma_d}{4}W>\frac{W}{4e},
\qquad
\alpha_C(\mathbf p_*)=\gamma_d\rho^d.
\]
For \(n\ge20\), one moreover has
\(\rho<1-1/(16n)\) and
\(\alpha_C(\mathbf p_*)<\gamma_d e^{-n/16}\),
so these rational points are not fiber centroids.

For the cube-pyramid body there is a stronger specified point. Let \(\tau\in(0,d)\) be the unique solution of
\[
\sum_{\mathbf z\in D_+}
\left(A_{\mathbf z}^d-\left(1-\frac\tau d\right)^d\right)_+
=\frac W2.
\]
Then \(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{height}}=(\mathbf0,\tau,\mathbf0)\in S\) satisfies
\(h_S(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{height}})\ge W/4\).
For \(n\ge20\), it also is not a fiber centroid.

The original even-dimensional simplex specialization is obtained by taking even \(n\ge2\), \(L=n^2\), and \(R=n^3\). It has, for every positive fiber, the explicit uniform estimate
\[
\frac{\sup_{\mathbf j\in D_+}h_S((\mathbf j,\mathbf c_{\mathbf j}))}{2^{-n}W}
\le e^3\left(\frac{2\pi e^3}{n}\right)^{n/2}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Its closed-form rational point
\(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{exp}}=(\mathbf0,q_n\mathbf1_d/(d+1))\), where
\(q_n=1-1/(2n)\), is not a fiber centroid and satisfies
\[
h_S(\mathbf p_{\mathrm{exp}})\ge\frac{W}{e^4n}
\ge\frac2{e^4}\,2^{-n}W.
\]
The source scalar \(q\) is denoted \(q_n\) here to distinguish it from the affine selector \(q(\cdot)\) in the accepted predecessor. For even \(n\ge20\), this same simplex body also satisfies the stronger all-locally-deep-point estimate and the constant-depth weighted-median conclusion above.

Finally, the rational simplex polytope
\[
\widehat C^\Delta_{n,L}
=\operatorname{conv}\left\{
(\mathbf z,\mathbf0),(\mathbf z,A_{\mathbf z}\mathbf e_i):
\mathbf z\in D,\ 1\le i\le d\right\}
\]
has exactly the same complete lattice fiber table as \(C^\Delta_{n,L}\), hence exactly the same \(S\), local depths, and ambient depths. Taking \(L=n\) gives the convex-hull formulation with \(A_{\mathbf z}=1-\|\mathbf z\|_2^2/n^4\); taking \(L=n^2\) gives the original larger-radius scale. Replacing \(\Phi_R(\mathbf x)\) by \(\|\mathbf x\|_2^2\) in either displayed body also leaves every lattice fiber unchanged. Any positive dilation \((\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\mapsto(\mathbf x,\lambda\mathbf y)\) preserves \(\alpha_C\) and every ratio \(h_S/W\), with the specified points transported by the same map; rational \(\lambda\), in particular \(\lambda=d\), preserves rationality of the polytopes.
